=== SCRIPT ===
## Midnight at the Gate
Midnight at the Gibraltar frontier. To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
The Rock sits at the western gate of the Mediterranean.
Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
This is why everyone fought over it, told from both sides' records.
[On screen: "A history explainer · every date sourced · British and Spanish records side by side · Facts as of 18 Oct 2026"]
[On screen: number card "14 sieges · 1309–1783" — "Sayer 1862 · García Sanz 2022 · Gibraltar National Museum"]
In 1782, ten floating batteries came to break it.
In 1941, a runway was laid across the only road to Spain.
So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?

## 1704: A Rock Changes Hands
Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
That summer, their fleet sailed into the Bay of Gibraltar.
Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of "Charles the Third."
This plan, printed in 1705, shows the prize: a walled town that historians on both sides would call the key of the Mediterranean.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «la preciosa llave del Mediterráneo» — "the precious key of the Mediterranean" · Sayer, 1862: "the key of the Mediterranean"]
Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender. The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «con cien hombres de guarnición … no había artilleros que las sirvieran» — "a garrison of a hundred men … there were no gunners to serve them"]
On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered. English histories say the twenty-fourth of July, on the old calendar.
British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third." Almost all of them left. By Spanish accounts, most settled a league to the north-east, at San Roque.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se habia acampado en las haciendas cercanas á la ermita de San Roque» — "had camped on the farms near the hermitage of San Roque"]
In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht made it permanent: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever." But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain says Gibraltar includes it.
Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727. Neither siege took it.
So in 1730, Philip the Fifth ordered a stone line across the isthmus, out of gun range, to cut Gibraltar off by land. The town behind it is still called La Línea: "the line."
[On screen: Gómez Nadal (Almoraima), on Philip V's order of 8 Oct 1730: «bloquear definitivamente la correspondencia y paso a la plaza por tierra» — "to block, once and for all, all contact with and passage to the town by land"]

## The Great Siege
Half a century later came a different question: can you starve a rock? On the twenty-first of June 1779, Madrid closed every link with Gibraltar.
Spain had joined France in its war with Britain. By autumn, about fourteen thousand men faced the Rock across the isthmus.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Carlos III declaró la guerra á Inglaterra y se unió á Francia» — "Charles III declared war on England and joined France"]
At sea, from mid-July, a Spanish squadron sealed the port. Its boats at Algeciras had one job: to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «encaminado principalmente á privar a la plaza de los viveres que le llegaban de las costas de África» — "aimed above all at depriving the town of the food that reached it from the coasts of Africa"]
By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many; an egg cost sixpence.
The governor, General Eliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea.
To break the blockade, Britain sent three relief fleets: 1780, 1781, 1782.
Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship full of lemons was brought in.
On the twelfth of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor, and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town. The townspeople fled south.
Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
By September 1782, about seven and a half thousand men held the Rock.
The garrison's answer was heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire. On the eighth of September, they used them in earnest against the Spanish works.
Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets sailed in, under the Duc de Crillon: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
[On screen: Fernández Duro, Armada española (1901): «alegrando la vista los 50 navios que se juntaron en Algeciras» — "the 50 ships of the line that gathered at Algeciras, a joy to see"]
Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
[On screen: Conseil de guerre privé (1785): «l'expérience que l'inventeur avoit demandée … à l'épreuve des boulets rouges» — "the test the inventor had asked for … against red-hot shot"]
The thirteenth of September 1782. At half past nine, the batteries moved into position. At a quarter to ten, the garrison opened fire. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, some four hundred guns answered together. By the next morning, all ten batteries were gone.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «á las diez y veinte y cinco minutos de la mañana … rompieron á un tiempo el fuego» — "at twenty-five past ten in the morning … opened fire all at once"]
More than two thousand attackers were lost, by British and Spanish counts; three hundred and fifty-seven were rescued.
[On screen: number card: "> 2,000 lost, prisoners included — British estimate & Montero (Spain)" · "185 hit by gunfire before the fires — French account, 1785" · "357 rescued — British return" · "Garrison: 16 killed — its own return" {S069} {S070} {S071}]
All that summer, the garrison had also been digging through the north face. By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
In July they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se formó un boquete tan grande … que pareció bien colocar en el un cañón» — "an opening was made so large … that it seemed right to place a cannon in it"]
The Rock was never starved out. In February 1783, word came of a preliminary peace, and on the fifth, the last shot was fired.
From all causes, Montero put the losses near two thousand inside and six thousand outside. The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and seventy dead. Gibraltar stayed British.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Los últimos sufrieron una pérdida de cerca de dos mil hombres. La nuestra se aproximó á seis mil por todas causas» — "The latter [the besieged] suffered a loss of nearly two thousand men. Ours came close to six thousand, from all causes" · number card: "Garrison return (Drinkwater): 333 killed or died of wounds · 536 died of sickness (scurvy deaths 1779–80 not included)"]

## The Neutral Ground
Which leaves a question the treaty never answered: where does the Rock end? Between the walls and the Spanish line lay a strip of sand: the neutral ground.
In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
[On screen: Gómez de Avellaneda: «con autorización española, fueran destruidos por los ingleses» — "with Spanish authorisation, they were destroyed by the British" · "Montero gives 1811"]
After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «el progresivo avance de la frontera sobre la zona neutral» — "the gradual advance of the frontier over the neutral zone"]
On the Spanish side, a town grew up behind the old line. In 1870, it became La Línea de la Concepción.
Remember this street. We'll come back to it.
This was the gap between them: open sand, between two towns.
In 1908, Britain told Spain, "as an act of courtesy," that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground. The fence went up in 1909; Spain has never recognised it as a border.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «"como acto de cortesía"» — "as an act of courtesy"]
Behind the fence: a garrison camp, gardens, rifle ranges, a racecourse.
And in 1934, part of the old racecourse became a grass airstrip. Subscribe if you'd like the next place in this series.

## A Runway on the Isthmus
Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself. Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway; in 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain.
[On screen: Spanish government to its London ambassador, 4 Mar 1939 (Marquina Barrio, 1981): «una porción usurpada del territorio nacional» — "a usurped portion of the national territory"]
Then Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels.
Those tunnels became a city inside the Rock: a road about a mile long, a hospital, a power station, dug by British and Canadian tunnellers.
Today, the tunnels add up to about fifty-five kilometres, more than the roads above ground.
This 1943 US Army map shows the town house by house, and the runway reaching into the bay.
June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier. Gibraltar sends its women and children away. By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.
[silent shot]
For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested British ships in its waters, but not the airstrip.
[On screen: Marquina Barrio, 1981: «no queda constancia de reclamaciones por el uso de la pista» — "there is no record of complaints over the use of the strip"]
On the night of the seventh of November 1942, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway. The invasion fleets, from Britain and the United States, came through the Strait.

## The Gate
After the war, the argument returned to the gate. In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
Some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers were cut off. The gate fully reopened in 1985.
The same square, today. In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand. People on foot still cross the runway.
And on the other side of the gate.
Remember this street? In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
That divides by the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs. Our read: the rich-looking number partly rests on the other side.
In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty to take the checks off this border.
It says it changes neither side's position on sovereignty. The old fence is coming down, but a new one stands a few metres behind it, with about a hundred and fifty metres left open.
As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is provisional, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
So why did everyone fight over this place? Where it sits, and the sea that could feed it. A wall in 1704. A line in 1730. A fence in 1909. A runway in 1941.
[silent shot]
In 1730, Spain built a line to cut the Rock off by land. Today, four in ten of the Rock's jobs are held by people who live beyond it. The last siege ended in 1783. The argument didn't. Next in Contested Places: London, 1666.
